summary: Mount Pope near Fort St. James: a Forest Service fire lookout from the 1920s, removed in 1972; the summit now has a gazebo and the park is day-use.

facts.status_note: BC Parks says the Forest Service fire lookout was removed in 1972. A gazebo stands at the summit. A hiking guide describes an old lookout there, which conflicts with BC Parks.

access.note: BC Parks describes Mount Pope Park as a day-use park with a hiking trail to the peak.

visit.trail_note: 6.5 km hiking trail to the peak. Trailhead parking is 4 km down Stones Bay Road, reached through Fort St. James.

events.note: Lookout use began in the 1920s, when a telegraph line was put in and the peak became a Forest Service fire lookout. BC Parks gives only the decade, so 1920 stands in for it.
Fire lookout removed. BC Parks gives the year only.
Trail to the peak designated a recreational trail.
Mount Pope Park established in January 2001.

evidence.supports: Location: about 7 km northwest of Fort St. James, northeast side of Stuart Lake
evidence.quote: Mount Pope is located about 7 km northwest of Fort St. James on the northeast side of Stuart Lake.

evidence.supports: Canada Lookouts files the site under Bulkley-Nechako
Canada Lookouts lists the site among British Columbia lookouts
Carrier people made the first trails up the peak
evidence.quote: The Carrier Native Indians established the first trails up Mount Pope.

evidence.supports: View to the north and early notice of hostile parties on Stuart Lake
evidence.quote: From the vantage point at the peak they could see far to the north and had advanced warning of any hostile parties coming down Stuart Lake.

evidence.supports: BC Parks account: Pope surveying for the Overland Telegraph Line in 1865
evidence.quote: In 1865 Major Franklin L. Pope was surveying a route for the Overland Telegraph Line.

evidence.supports: BC Parks account: Pope separated from his party and spent a night alone on the mountain
evidence.quote: He was separated from his party and had to spend the night alone on the mountain, which became known as Mount Pope thereafter.

evidence.supports: 1928 letter quoted in the provincial name record
Letter account: Pope wintered with the HBC (Hudson's Bay Company; the letter prints only HBC) at Takla Lake and wished to climb the mountain while passing
evidence.quote: Major Pope wintered with the HBC at Takla Lake and when passing here, wished to climb this mountain.

evidence.supports: Letter account: Pope remained out all night before reaching the peak
evidence.quote: old Major Pope was so tired that he remained out all night, reaching the peak only the next morning

evidence.supports: 1920s telegraph line and use as a Forest Service fire lookout
evidence.quote: In the 1920s a telegraph line was put in when once again the peak was in use as a lookout point, this time as a Forest Service fire lookout.

evidence.supports: Lookout removed in 1972; trail designated recreational in 1983
evidence.quote: The lookout was removed in 1972 and the trail to the peak was designated as recreational trail in 1983.
Mount Pope Park was established in January of 2001.

evidence.supports: Gazebo at the peak with a 360-degree view (BC Parks; no mention of a tower on the page)
evidence.quote: A gazebo is available at the peak of Mount Pope. This is an ideal spot to have a snack and enjoy the 360 degree view.

evidence.supports: Hiking guide describes an old forestry lookout and gazebo at the summit (conflicts with BC Parks)
evidence.quote: Steep trail up to an old forestry lookout and gazebo with views of Stuart Lake and the surrounding ranges.

evidence.supports: Day-use park popular with hikers and climbers
evidence.quote: Mount Pope is a day-use park popular with hikers and rockclimbers.
A 6.5 km hiking trail to the peak provides a panoramic view of Stuart Lake and the mountains to the north.

evidence.supports: Trailhead 4 km down Stones Bay Road
evidence.quote: The trailhead parking lot is 4 km down Stones Bay Road on the right.

evidence.supports: Route: drive through Fort St. James on Stuart Drive W, then turn left (west) onto Stones Bay Road
evidence.quote: Proceed through Fort St. James on Stuart Drive W and turn left (west) on Stones Bay Road.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: BC Parks says the lookout was removed in 1972 and describes only a gazebo at the peak. A hiking guide describes an old forestry lookout and gazebo at the summit. The story follows BC Parks, the managing agency, and reports the guide's description.

BC Parks links the name to Major Franklin L. Pope's 1865 survey for the Overland Telegraph Line. A 1928 letter quoted in the BC Geographical Names record places Pope at Takla Lake in the winter. Both accounts have him spending a night on the mountain. The story gives both.

notes_for_editor: The lookout dates (1920s use, 1972 removal, 1983 trail, 2001 park) rest on one source, the history section of the BC Parks root page. The /nature-culture page returned 404 in the crawl, so the root page is cited. The 1920 event year stands in for the decade. No staffing record, lookout design or height was found, so none is given. Brief status and access were unknown and are filled from BC Parks. Brief coordinates match the Canada Lookouts record and BC Parks' location. BC Parks places the park in the Omineca region; the brief and Canada Lookouts say Bulkley-Nechako. The brief local_unit is kept as given and the regional district was not checked. On the 2026-10-20 fact-check, the BC Parks page was searched and does not mention a tower. The letter on BC Geographical Names prints HBC only; the story expands it as Hudson's Bay Company, the standard reading.
